item.title: When Does Sharing Locations Become Surveillance?
item.description:
Parenting

When Does Sharing Locations Become Surveillance?

52% of parents report tracking their young adult child's location.

Posted June 26, 2026

Key points
  • The majority of parents use location tracking with their 18-25 year-old children.
  • Parents track their adult children because they are worried about them and it gives them peace of mind.
  • The Test of Four indicates location tracking of a 18-25 year-old child is overindulgence called overnurture.
  • Adulting is challenging and tracking can prevent taking accountability for one's well-being.

Today's parents have at their disposal technology that allows them to know where their children are almost every moment of the day. Most parents say the reason for tracking their young adult child is "safety." But when does tracking turn from "safety" into "surveillance?" Is this a good thing or a bad thing? Does location tracking help or hinder the adulting process?

  • Do you worry about what your young adult children (age 18-25) are doing when you are not around to advise them?
  • Do you use location tracking with your young adult daughters more than your sons?
  • Why do you use location tracking with your young adult children? How does it make you feel?
Source: Ketut Subiyanto/Pexels

Who Are Emerging Adults?

The concept of emerging adulthood is a period of development between ages 18 and 25, first proposed by Jeffrey Arnett (2000). This stage only exists in cultures like ours that allow young people a prolonged period of independent role exploration during their late teens and early twenties. Emerging adulthood is a time in which they actively explore different life roles, values, and lifestyles.

Arnett says, "...emerging adulthood is neither adolescence nor young adulthood but is theoretically and empirically distinct from them both. Emerging adulthood is distinguished by relative independence from social roles and from normative expectations."

They are in between. Sometimes emerging adults see themselves as adolescents, and sometimes as adults. This makes "adulting" a difficult challenge.

What Is Adulting?

Kelly Williams Brown is credited with coining the term "adulting" in her 2013 book titled Adulting: How to Become a Grown-up in 535 Easy(ish) Steps. Here are some ways this concept is defined:

  • "Adulting is the practice of behaving with the characteristics of a responsible adult, especially completing everyday essential tasks" (Houy, 2023).
  • "Adulting is the assumption of tasks, responsibilities, and behaviors traditionally associated with normal grown-up life, along with the implication that the individual in question does not particularly identify as an adult and that acting as one does not come naturally" (Wigmore, 2023).

Adulting is being able to complete routine tasks expected of an adult. Here are a few examples:

  • Holding down a full-time job
  • Regularly paying utility bills, taxes, phone, and internet bills
  • Paying for housing, monthly rent, or mortgage payments
  • Being responsible for food, clothing, and leisure
  • Doing routine chores

But for many emerging adults, "adulting" means more than doing routine chores and tasks; it involves taking total accountability for one's well-being, acknowledging one's boundaries, and effectively communicating one's needs.

Today's Technology Makes It Easy to Track Children

Today, everyone has a smartphone. If parents and their children have smartphones, they can track their child's whereabouts using the Find My app on an iPhone or the Google Family Link App on an Android device. Individual GPS tracking devices are also available, and most come with a monthly subscription.

How Many Parents Track Their Young Adult Children?

A little over half (52%) of parents report tracking their young adult child's location using a cell phone or similar device, according to a recent Mott Poll titled Safety or Surveillance: Tracking of Young Adults (Clark et al. 2026). Tracking occurred more often for young adults aged 18-20 compared to those aged 21-25. Also, more frequently for daughters than sons. Seventy-one percent of parents say the tracking feature is always on, while 29% say they use it only in certain situations.

  • if they are out late at night (44%),
  • in an unfamiliar place (39%),
  • using a rideshare or taxi service (25%), or
  • out with someone they don’t know (23%).

Why Do Parents Track Their Young Adult Children?

Source: Clark, et al./Used with permission C.S. Mott Children's Hospital National Poll on Children's Health

According to the poll, 95% of parents who track their young adult child’s location say it helps them worry less, 23% acknowledge it sometimes makes them more anxious than reassured. Additional reasons for tracking their young adult children were:

  • Peace of mind (68%)
  • An emergency (64%)
  • A good time to call (21%)
  • Catch up and stay current (17%)
  • Checking to see if they are in an approved place (9%).

Almost all of the adult children (96%) knew their parents were tracking them.

Sixty-five percent of parents that do not track feel it is an invasion of their child's privacy.

The Most Valuable Lessons in Life Come From Our Failures, Not Our Successes

I believe failures teach us the most valuable life lessons compared to our successes. When I failed, I stepped back from the incident. I analyzed what went wrong. I looked at the things I could have done differently to ensure success. I grew from the experience. When I had a big success, I felt good. I celebrated, and then moved on. I did not step back to take stock of myself and figure out exactly what I did or did not do that contributed to my success.

Consequently, if we jump in and rescue our children time and again, we rob them of learning some of life's most valuable lessons, especially by the time they become an emerging adult. Of the parents that do not track their children, 51% believe it may prevent their emerging adult child from becoming independent and responsible.

Is Tracking Your Young Adult a Form of Overindulgence?

Clarke et al. (2014) identify three types of childhood overindulgence:

  1. Too Much (giving children too much of everything)
  2. Overnurture (hovering, over-parenting, helicoptering, doing things children should be doing themselves)
  3. Soft Structure (not having rules or enforcing rules, soft boundaries, low expectations)

This is not about tracking 10, 12, or 14-year-olds. It's about parents tracking 18 to 25-year-olds. Location tracking feels like what Clarke et al. (2014) describe as overnurture. To find out, use the Test of Four.

Applying the Test of Four

The Test of Four is a tool that identifies overindulgence. Parents ask themselves four questions about their actions. Each question is based on overindulgence research. A “Yes” answer to one or more questions indicates overindulgence. Let's apply the Test of Four to location tracking of emerging adults.

  1. Does tracking my 18-25 year-old young adult children hinder them from learning developmental tasks? Yes. It can impede the development of independence. Independence involves making decisions without parental oversight. It can interfere with learning to keep oneself safe.
  2. Does location tracking use a disproportionate amount of family resources for one or more of my young adult children? No.
  3. Whose needs are being met? Does it benefit me the adult more than my 18-25 year-old child? Yes. According to the poll, 95% of parents who track their young adult child’s location say it helps them worry less, and 68% say it gives them peace of mind.
  4. Does it do harm to others, society, or the planet? No.

Adulting is challenging for an emerging adult (18-25 years-old). To take accountability for one's well-being, acknowledging one's boundaries, and effectively communicating one's needs they need to be allowed to spread their wings. Parents can provide a safety net, but at the same time, they need to let their young go.

Practice Aloha. Do all things with love, grace, and gratitude.

item.title: The End of (Coupled) Sex?
item.description:
Sex

The End of (Coupled) Sex?

Shifting norms, technology, and fear reshape how intimacy unfolds.

Posted June 26, 2026

Key points
  • Published in 1983, "The End of Sex" argued that the sexual revolution removed intimacy from sex.
  • "Men between the ages of 20 and 30 are spending less time outdoors than prison inmates right now."
  • 24% of men aged 22–34 reported having had no sex in the last year.

"I have finally come to see that every game has a rule, and sex has rules. Unless you play by the rules, you'll find sex can create a depth of loneliness that nothing else can." —George Leonard, The End of Sex

Source: G-Stock Studio/Shutterstock

Having taught about intimate relationships for more than a decade in the Leonard Pavilion at the Esalen Institute, I finally got around to reading a book by the man for whom the pavilion was named. Published in 1983, The End of Sex: Erotic Love After the Sexual Revolution argues that the sexual revolution produced a culture of physical gratification so efficiently delivered that it severed sex from anything resembling intimacy. Leonard's concern was that sex without real intimacy generates a particular type of loneliness, one that casual encounters can't cure and that multiplying partners only compounds. Unfortunately, George did not live to see the logical endpoint of his prognosis, which is that a significant portion of the population has stopped having coupled sex at all. And this isn’t because of some form of enlightenment à la Lenny Kravitz; it’s because they're scared, isolated, deluded by social media, and avoidant.

According to a study published in JAMA Network Open using General Social Survey data, the share of men aged 18–24 who reported no sex in the past year climbed from 19% in 2002 to 31 percent by 2018. More recent CDC data tells a grimmer story: by 2022–2023, 24% of men aged 22–34 reported having had no sex — up from just 9% a decade earlier. This is not a blip. From 2010 to 2024, the share of young adults reporting no sex in the past year doubled, from 12 to 24%, according to General Social Survey data compiled by the Institute for Family Studies.

In The Boy Crisis, Warren Farrell describes the sexual landscape that young men now must navigate: "His testosterone is surging with desire for perhaps half the girls in his class, but he fears that if he acts on his feelings too quickly, he's a sexual harasser; if he acts too slowly, he's a wimp." What Warren is saying is that there’s a subconscious communication of “momentum” that is nearly impossible to calculate using today's communications technology, such as texting.

And I know this is controversal, but for all the good that the #MeToo movement accomplished and all of the rapes that it prevented, the fear it has instilled in many men is tantamount to paralysis. In my clinical psychotherapy practice, I’ve seen so many young men who have effectively decommissioned their erotic lives out of genuine terror—terror of being accused of something horrific. They are not pursuing women in the ways that would once have been called “chivalrous” — and that I described as "The Myth of Romance" in my first book — because the former “games” of dating and romance have become amorphous. I cannot even get young patients to say, “We’re dating”—instead they say, “We’re hanging out,” which essentially means that they’ll tolerate their current lover until they can upgrade. The overcorrection of the #Metoo movement has left both sexes stranded on opposite shores of the same river, neither willing to swim across.

In Notes on Being a Man, Scott Galloway frames the structural cause like this: "Men between the ages of 20 and 30 are spending less time outdoors than prison inmates right now... You've put a casino, a porn site, an arcade, Netflix — you've put it all in their pocket or on their computer. The temptation to just stay at home and get that constant dopamine hit from all sorts of different receptors online is just more tempting than going out and doing stuff." He concludes that this is breeding “a new species of asocial, asexual males."

The data on what young people do when they are nominally together bears this out. A survey of 10,000 college students across 480 campuses found that 35 percent had either scrolled social media or sent a text message during sex. Are they looking at instructional videos on how the parts fit together???

For older adults, the journey is different but the destination is the same. Partnered sex past a certain age requires logistical coordination that would befuddle the Academy Award Governor's Ball event planner: synchronized schedules, negotiated emotional availability, location services, advance planning of hygiene and undergarments, and the mental fortitude of someone entering a cage match. The last time I witnessed organic passion was in a 1970s French film.

Into this void steps the solo practitioner. Masturbation is the only appointment that rarely cancels or disappoints. It doesn't ask you to be well-coiffed. It doesn't care if your underwear is pretty. It doesn't require emotional intelligence. It's the one relationship where you are not, in some fundamental sense, a problem. As I wrote in How to Survive Your Childhood Now That You're an Adult, behavioral pressure valves like this are baked into every civilization: we're semi-permitted certain peccadillos precisely because they keep us from storming the Bastille. In our current psychological dystopia, the beast with one back will have to suffice.

The loneliness epidemic that Galloway, Farrell, and a chorus of researchers are now documenting is not incidental to a sex recession. We have traded the risks of connection—and I’d argue that risks equal eroticism—for the safety of no connection, which is engendering an abyss of loneliness that is soul-crushing.

item.title: Heat Might Cloud Your Brain
item.description:
Environment

Heat Might Cloud Your Brain

Heat impairs cognition, and climate change could make it worse.

Posted June 26, 2026

Key points
  • Heat impairs memory, attention, and executive functions like problem-solving and decision-making.
  • People without AC performed measurably worse on cognitive tests during a heat wave.
  • Long-term heat exposure is linked to lasting cognitive decline across large populations.
  • Some models project a 5–7% drop in average human cognitive function due to heat by 2100.

Heat waves are becoming more common, with severe health consequences ranging from cardiovascular, respiratory, and renal difficulties to death due to extreme heat exposure or heat stroke. But even setting aside those direct risks, heat has severe indirect consequences. A large number of studies have shown that high temperatures impair cognitive functions, which in turn leads to poor decisions.

The reasons why high temperatures cloud your brain are probably related to changes in brain blood flow. When air temperature is too high, your body attempts to protect you by diverting blood and energy to cool you down, a process called thermoregulation. Unfortunately, this alters blood flow to the brain, and although the exact mechanisms are not yet fully understood, the consequences are not good. Heat also causes fatigue and sleep impairments, which compound the cognitive toll.

Your Brain Without AC

Cedeño Laurent and coauthors (2018) conducted a study on university students' cognitive functions during the 2016 heat wave in Boston, MA. Over 12 days in July, students completed two tests daily. One was a numerical task requiring addition or subtraction of two-digit numbers. The other was the Stroop task, a classic in cognitive psychology that measures the ability to inhibit impulses and direct attention.

What made the study particularly interesting is that some students lived in buildings with air conditioning (AC), while others did not. The AC group experienced temperatures in the 17–25°C range, averaging 21°C (70 °F). The non-AC group endured temperatures in the 20–30°C range, averaging 26°C (79 °F). That difference was enough: students in the non-AC group gave fewer correct responses per minute on the numerical task and were slower on the Stroop task.

Studies like this one have limitations, including small and specific samples (38 university students, in this case). But they have been accumulating over the years. Laboratory studies, in which people are randomly assigned to different ambient temperatures, have consistently found that those exposed to higher temperatures display impaired memory, reduced attention, and lower performance in executive functions, including problem-solving, understanding complex tasks, and decision-making. So, yes: heat might quite literally make you dumber.

Evidence Linking Long-term Heat Exposure to Cognitive Decline

We are also beginning to accumulate data from large panel studies. Yin and coauthors (2024) used data from the China Family Panel Study, tracking over 53,000 participants across eight years. The researchers examined the relationship between high-temperature exposure, defined as the proportion of time above 32°C (90°F), and cognitive test scores (verbal and mathematical) collected as part of the panel. The results show that both exposure to extreme temperatures and sustained, long-term exposure are associated with cognitive decline. On average, in the data, a 10% increase in the number of days with peak temperatures above 32°C was associated with a 2% drop in cognitive capacity.

That might not sound like much. But how many additional high-temperature days will we face in the near future? 10% more, or 40% more? Under standard climate-change scenarios, the study of Yin et al. concluded that average cognitive function in humans might decrease between 5 and 7% by 2100. That is a sobering prospect. The effects are also uneven: they are worse for the elderly, for people with high body-mass index, and for males compared to females. And the long-term averages do not capture everything. In the data of Yin et al., a high proportion of extreme-temperature hours in the days before a test was already associated with declined cognition, meaning that a single heat wave may leave your brain clouded for some time afterward.

Practical Strategies During Heat Waves

As discussed in a previous post, carrying too much in your mind (what psychologists call “cognitive load”) can lead to poor decisions. That is why "multi-tasking" is a bad idea, and you should single-task instead. Financial worries cloud judgment in much the same way, which is the reason that poverty is often found to cloud your brain. The mechanism behind heat-impaired judgment is different and more directly physiological. But the practical takeaways are similar.

The old expression “in the heat of the moment” usually refers to poor choices driven by strong emotions, but it turns out to hold more literally as well. As climate change makes heat waves more frequent and high-temperature days more frequent, you should be wary of when and how you make decisions. Beware of decisions made during or shortly after a heat wave.

Avoid important decisions on high-temperature days when you can. Maybe you should delay buying that big-ticket item if it's a hot day (unless it is an AC system!). As always with consequential choices, give yourself time. Do not trust your gut. Check your reasoning carefully. Seek outside advice. Wait until you can achieve some emotional and cognitive distance.

And if it is hot outside and you have to make an important decision, cool down first.

item.title: Neurodiversity: Beyond "Differently Wired"
item.description:
Neurodiversity

Neurodiversity: Beyond "Differently Wired"

How the neurodiversity movement reproduces the problems of the medical model.

Posted June 26, 2026

Key points
  • Neurodiversity has helped many people feel less pathologized and more understood.
  • However, replacing disorder with neurotypes leaves the assumptions of the medical model intact.
  • The language of neurotypes has transformed descriptions into identities.
  • Relational, developmental, and social explanations can be eclipsed by neurocentric thinking.
Source: AI-Generated / ChatGPT

Over the past decade, the neurodiversity movement has transformed the mental health discourse. Originally developed as a challenge to pathologizing narratives around such psychiatric diagnoses as autism and ADHD, its “umbrella” has come to cover an increasingly large and diverse portion of the population. While the neurodiversity paradigm contains a range of different perspectives, its mainstream form is characterized by the claim that the experiences and patterns of behavior falling under its umbrella are best understood as expressions of neurological difference, a natural part of human variation, as opposed to representing some sort of dysfunction, disorder, or disease process as psychiatry has long held.

In certain respects, this shift has been valuable: it has challenged stigma associated with the experiences and behaviors that come under such diagnostic labels; it has also promoted an expansion and acceptance of human difference more generally; and, finally, it has called into question the central psychiatric premise that psychological distress and impairment are properly thought of as “medical disorders.” Perhaps most impactfully, the language of neurodiversity has provided a sense of dignity and community for some, as well as a common language that provides a way of interpreting and articulating their struggles and having those struggles recognized by others.

Despite these contributions, however, there are important reasons to question the neurodiversity paradigm. At a time, now, where it dominates mental health discourse and has a significant say in how many people understand their own minds, it has gone far beyond a non-pathologizing recategorization of a very small sub-group of people.

Chief among these reasons is that while it presents itself as a critique of—and departure from—the medical model, it nevertheless retains its cardinal assumption: the belief that psychological distress and impairment are best explained in terms of individual, internal factors, and in the case of such diagnoses as ADHD and autism, that such processes are reducible to neurology. This is in direct contrast to accounts that emphasize social and relational explanations of psychological distress.

From Disorder to Neurotype

Where psychiatry, directly or indirectly, locates the source of distress or impairment in a disordered brain (i.e., neurodevelopmental disorder), neurodiversity theory tends to locate it in a differently wired brain, in terms of different “neurotypes.” This is often portrayed as a radical shift. But how radical is it?

It is radical in one sense, but highly conservative in another, as it uncritically accepts psychiatric categorization itself and, in the case of autism and ADHD, the assumption that the experiences and behaviors gathered under these categories are best explained in neurological terms. In other words, it replaces one form of essentialism with another. Although the moral evaluation changes—from deficit to difference—the underlying explanatory framework remains intact. This is important because, while neurological explanations are often presented as settled science, there remains considerable debate about whether the categories in question correspond to discrete neurological entities at all.

The Problem of Reification

Psychologists have long warned against reification: the tendency to treat abstract concepts as though they were concrete things. Diagnostic categories are particularly vulnerable to this error. For more than a century, psychiatry has sought to overcome the problem by grounding its diagnostic categories in biology. The hope was that advances in neuroscience and genetics would eventually reveal the underlying disease processes responsible for psychiatric diagnoses.

However, despite enormous investment and decades of research, this project has failed to identify specific biological markers that reliably correspond to the vast majority of psychiatric categories, including ADHD and autism. This failure has prompted a noticeable shift in tone within sections of the psychiatric establishment. In a recent article for the New York Times, the influential psychiatrist Awais Aftab put it this way:

“When psychiatrists say that you ‘have A.D.H.D.,’ what they really mean is something like this: After spending time listening to you, talking with people who know you and observing how you think and behave, I’ve made a judgment call that your experience fits a behavioural pattern we currently call A.D.H.D… Patterns like these are handy for picking treatments that might be helpful, but they don’t settle the deeper questions about how your brain works or what kind of person you are.”

This statement is as honest as it is revealing. Psychiatric categories, in other words, have been—and continue to be—wrongly reified. To say that someone has ADHD or has autism is to offer a particular way of describing a complex constellation of behaviors, feelings, relationships, and life experiences, as interpreted through a psychiatric lens. It is not to identify a thing that people “have”—a disordered or differently wired brain—something that, despite what many have been led to believe, has not been empirically established.

As Aftab goes on to acknowledge, psychiatry has often “given the false impression that each mental disorder is a relatively distinct problem with clear boundaries and an essence that makes it what it is,” when in fact such categories are “practical tools that provide a shared language.” Aftab deserves credit for saying the quiet part out loud. Yet in doing so, he also exposes psychiatry to a range of difficult questions concerning the ontological status of its categories and the authority granted to them.

Here, however, we are concerned specifically with the neurodiversity movement and its use of psychiatric categories. In my view, and in the view of many critical colleagues, the neurodiversity movement rightly challenges the pathologizing assumptions attached to the experiences that tend to be diagnosed as ADHD and autism—particularly under the considerably broadened definitions of the DSM-5. Yet by affirming rather than questioning these categories, neurodiversity theory has perpetuated and, in some respects, amplified their reification beyond psychiatry itself.

The result is that what Aftab describes as “practical tools” have increasingly become treated as defining features of personhood—a leap from description to cause, and from interpretation to identity. In doing so—and this is the central concern—the relational, developmental, and socio-cultural dimensions of human life risk being eclipsed by an individualistic and neuro-centric conception of what it means to be a person in such cases.

What Happens to Social and Relational Explanations?

Interpretation is inherently subjective, and subjectivity is strongly shaped by socio-cultural influences, pressures, and trends. Psychiatric diagnoses, by their nature, therefore encompass heterogeneous groups of people whose difficulties may arise through a wide range of developmental, relational, social, and/or biological pathways, which may, in important respects, constitute very different sets of experiences. This is an inevitable consequence of using categories that lack objective validation.

Which diagnosis a person receives—or adopts for themselves—is significantly influenced by the prevailing discourse surrounding psychological distress at a given historical moment. This helps explain the dramatic rise and fall of particular diagnoses over time (e.g., multiple personality disorder, borderline personality disorder, and bipolar disorder). The psychiatric categories that fall under the neurodiversity umbrella—principally autism and ADHD—are no different in this respect. Indeed, as the broadened definitions of the DSM-5 have taken hold, and as public interest in neurodiversity has grown—with services, identities, and communities increasingly organized around these categories—more and more of the heterogeneity of human distress and impairment has come to be located within them.

Given the widespread belief that autism and ADHD identify fixed neurological differences, a deep concern is that experiences that might previously have been understood through the lenses of social adversity, attachment difficulties, developmental trauma, or complex PTSD are increasingly being interpreted through neurological frameworks. What appears, from a psychiatric or neurodiversity perspective, as evidence of an underlying neurological disorder or difference may, from another standpoint, be understood as an adaptive response to chronic relational adversity or adverse social conditions.

As such, like the biomedical model it originally sought to challenge, neurodiversity theory can divert attention away from the interpersonal and societal conditions that shape human experience. When difficulties are understood primarily as expressions of an underlying neurotype—just as when they are understood in terms of a disordered brain—there is a risk that relational trauma, attachment disruptions, family dynamics, poverty, exclusion, discrimination, and other forms of social injustice recede into the background, exonerating relationships, institutions, and society from critical scrutiny. This deep problem of the medical model, in other words, persists in the model of neurodiversity.

Conclusion

If psychiatric diagnoses are interpretative constructs rather than natural kinds, then replacing the language of disorder with that of neurotype does not, by itself, move us beyond the medical model or some of the central problems associated with it. This is not to deny the reality of human difference or the value that many people find in neurodiversity as a source of identity, meaning, and community.

Rather, it is to question whether categories that remain scientifically contested and interpretatively constructed should occupy the privileged explanatory position they increasingly do, often at the expense of relational, developmental, and social understandings of human suffering. The central question is not whether people differ; it is whether our differences and difficulties are best understood in terms of the kinds of brains we are presumed to possess or in terms of the relationships, histories, and social worlds through which our lives are constituted.

item.title: Family Happiness Through Mindful Awareness
item.description:
Mindfulness

Family Happiness Through Mindful Awareness

Building intention, awareness, and compassion for greater connection.

Posted June 26, 2026

Key points
  • Family resilience and well being rely on acknowleding the stresses and joys of life, real time.
  • Contemplative practice builds skills that help us skilfully relate to whatever our family experiences.
  • Mindfulness may seem trendy, but it is a practical way to support awareness, compassion and intention.
  • Cultivating habits that support clear-seeing, intention and compassion changes life for us - and our families.

Mindfulness has become such an overused buzzword that people’s eyes sometimes glaze over when they hear it. Dismissing it has become a fad of its own. But mindfulness isn’t a cure-all or trend; it’s one of many contemplative practices for developing traits like resilience and empathy. The bigger picture is what matters: In an uncertain, changing world, how can we learn to live skillfully, with more awareness, patience, and kindness?

Source: merve / pexels

One useful habit, as you hear anything new, is to ask yourself: Is it true? Is it true that family life tends to be busy, changing, and sometimes difficult? In the face of those experiences, we get caught up in living reactively, without much awareness or intention. We run on autopilot, sticking with habitual beliefs and behaviors that don’t move us usefully forward.

We can instead develop cognitive abilities that let us meet our reality with more ease. It takes practice and effort, but it’s open to anyone. What follows goes beyond mindfulness into insight: exploring how the mind actually works. Think of it as a toolkit for recognizing common ways of living and building more useful ones.

  1. Start by paying attention. We spend much of our lives distracted, missing what’s right in front of us. One Harvard study found that the simple act of paying attention increases our happiness. Staying present is the start of any real communication, too; our kids and partners notice when we’re not attending to them. We’ll still get distracted often, but it helps to get better at paying attention, and to notice when we’ve drifted.

    Meditation: A concentration practice from Mark Bertin on Insight Timer.

  2. Attention leads to awareness. Awareness grows out of attention. This is the mindfulness part: The ability to see clearly, without bias, what’s happening right now. If the word ‘mindfulness’ shuts you down, ask yourself: Is it true I’m better off knowing what’s going on, real time, in my life? For instance, catching anger as it rises, instead of only realizing afterward we’ve snapped at our child once again, creates room for a more nuanced response. Awareness also reveals various filters we tend to see the world through, as well as assumptions about happiness, emotion, and much more that aren’t all that accurate (see Laurie Santos’s Science of Well-Being course).

    Meditation: An open awareness practice from Mark Coleman.

  3. Awareness allows for change. We can all cultivate new habits, once we notice we have habits at all. For example, we develop routine ways to meet challenges, from misbehavior to homework routines and everything in between. Start with anger again, where the only option might feel like lashing out or swallowing it. Maybe someone failed a test. In the past, confrontation about study habits led to defensiveness and shut down, and nothing changed. If we recognize early how anger feels in our body, nuance our emotional experience (maybe we’re frustrated because we feel powerless, or scared about long-term academics), and pause before reacting (a skill built through meditation), new and creative paths forward reveal themselves (see Lisa Feldman Barrett’s website about emotions).

    Meditation: Tara Brach’s RAIN practice.

  4. Awareness builds resilience. Most of us don’t mentally treat ourselves as kindly as we’d treat anyone else, a habit so common it has been described for centuries. That constant self-criticism breeds unhappiness, defensiveness, and influences how we treat others. Recognizing our inner critic as an old impersonal habit, and practicing self-compassion, has well-documented benefits, including less burnout and better persistence when things get difficult (see research on Kristin Neff’s self-compassion site). Less self-criticism changes how we feel and act as parents, while modeling the same powerful mindset for our children.

    Meditation: A self-compassion practice from Kristin Neff.

  5. Awareness builds compassion. Exploring our experience through this lens, we can also recognize that everyone else struggles to find happiness, everyone has an inner critic, and everyone faces change and uncertainty. Without condoning anyone’s behavior, we can cultivate the belief that every person, everywhere, simply wants to be happy and at ease. A struggling teen may seem angry or apathetic but of course doesn’t want to be struggling. That recognition naturally softens how we meet them.

    Meditation: A lovingkindness practice from Mark Bertin.

  6. Awareness and compassion benefit people around us. As we grow more attentive, more aware of our habits, and more empathetic, we engage differently with the world. We stay present, patient, and empathetic, and therefore stay in touch with our best intentions. That desire to influence our families and the world around us for the better is the bigger picture of contemplative practice.

A fundamental teaching of insight meditation is that one thing leads to another: how we meet a moment shapes what comes next. Approach a problem tangled in reactivity and bias, and that colors how it unfolds. Approach a difficult person while grounded in awareness and compassion, including moments our kids feel challenging, and the whole conversation shifts. Contemplative practice, including mindfulness, isn’t self-help or a fad. It certainly may help us feel better, but in its heart, it supports everyone around us too.

Take Action – Resilient Parent, Resilient Child

If any of this makes sense to you, select a practice and commit to it. Approach it as practice. The intention is not shutting off thinking or scary calmness. Life pushes us into distraction, reactivity and autopilot. If you experience that and stick with practice anyway, that’s perfect.

Set aside a few minutes a day. Let go of short-term goals. Through that effort and repetition, useful perspectives and skills become more accessible outside of meditation.

  1. Choose a meditation app. Guided practices are easier at the start for most people. Use an app like the Insight Meditation Timer or seek out a local meditation group.
  2. Let go of preconceived notions of meditation. Don’t expect instant relaxation or a quiet mind.
  3. Schedule a time daily. Open-ended plans (sometime tomorrow) rarely work with a new habit.
  4. Stay patient when you forget to practice. It’s hard forming a new habit.
  5. Stay patient with your busy mind. Exploring how we relate to thoughts and emotions is an intention of practice, not eliminating them.
  6. Commit to both your contemplative practice and to living intentionally. See what happens over time when you commit to more awareness and compassion in your life.

item.title: The Relationships Your Future Brain Is Counting On
item.description:
Aging

The Relationships Your Future Brain Is Counting On

The brain-healthy significance of making social investments now.

Posted June 26, 2026

Key points
  • Are you taking steps now to invest in relationships with others who can help support you when you are older?
  • We need both solitude and community for quality brain health.
  • There are negative brain health implications of solo aging.
  • We should ask ourselves, to whom are we visible? Who would notice if we needed support?

Many of us understand the importance of protecting our brains from too much stress, poor sleep, and unhealthy diets. However, we may not devote enough time to considerations of our future relationships. The social connections we cultivate today may become a component of the strongest forms of brain care we have decades from now. Our brains weren’t designed to choose between having healthy solitude and having healthy community. Our brains flourish when we intentionally make room for both.

Healthy Solitude

Previously, I’ve written about the need to unplug from various technologies and the need to avoid feeling obligated to always be available (e.g., responding immediately to text messages, emails, calls). Choosing solitude over these stressful social obligations is healthy. It gives our brains time for more opportunities to experience “soft fascination,” as I also wrote about in a previous post.

Therefore, I want it to be clear that our brains can benefit from solitude, especially when in nature or in silent reflection. The benefits can manifest as attention recovery, greater self-awareness, and enhanced mental restoration. Yet because our brains are social as much as physical, we must also be proactively mindful of what we currently deposit into our social accounts for our future self.

Togetherness must increasingly today be intentional for the good of our cognitive and emotional health.
Source: Nick Fewing/Unsplash

Healthy Connection

In her book Essential Retirement Planning for Solo Agers, Dr. Sara Z. Geber uses the terms “solo ager” and “solo aging” to highlight the special needs of people aging alone without a spouse, adult children, or other family support. Some people may not even have fictive kin: nonbiological relatives who feel like family and can be a part of their support system when needed in later life. This isn’t necessarily the fault of a solo ager. Life sometimes just happens.

However, before becoming an older adult, we can be mindful of the benefits of investing in social relationships. Most discussions of the implications of solo aging focus on finances, housing, or medical planning. What gets overlooked is the brain-health implications of solo aging and social invisibility.

It's never too early to begin to think about social connection as a healthy choice for the aging brain.
Source: Rodrigo Gonzalez/Unsplash

Social Invisibility vs. Visibility

Ask yourself: Who is it that sees you? To whom are you visible? What are you doing to sustain relationships with those persons?

Most of us prepare for or at least think about the financial aspects of aging. We are often less likely to prepare for the social aspects of aging. Unfortunately, this may be one of the biggest blind spots in protecting our future brain health.

Isolation is not what humans need; social connection continues to be vital as we age. Staying connected relates to how well we think, feel, and thrive as we grow older. Some people may never consider who will notice if they begin to physically, cognitively, or emotionally struggle. Yet our brains may depend on this answer more than we realize.

Your future brain health may depend as much on who knows you as on how well you care for yourself now. Thus, one of the most important investments you make for your future brain isn’t solely choosing another healthy habit but perhaps prioritizing developing another meaningful relationship. The cultural shift of the modern world has turned humans to their phones and computers as a default, often to the detriment of seeing and engaging with others around us. Therefore, the initiation and nurturance of meaningful relationships now has to be more intentional for the health of our brains.

The healthiest brains need moments of quiet, but they also need people who will notice when they’ve been quiet for too long, anxious, or otherwise struggling. This is more apt to occur in sustained authentic togetherness. Our brain health is improved by being known and noticed by significant others, sharing in laughter, emotional support, cognitive stimulation through conversation, and having people who can recognize subtle changes over time.

Although we cannot predict who will one day become a solo ager, we can decide today what kind of social life we intentionally build. Every meaningful conversation, every friendship we maintain, every neighbor we come to know, every family member we call is more than an act of kindness. It is an investment in the health of two brains, ours and theirs, that has longstanding, potentially positive consequences.

item.title: How to Deal with a Date Who 'Summer Shades'
item.description:
Mating

How to Deal with a Date Who 'Summer Shades'

The person you are dating may use this shady practice rather than break up.

Posted June 26, 2026

Key points
  • Summer shading: When the person you are dating deliberately pulls away from you during the Summer months.
  • This allows your significant other to enjoy being "single" while at the same time keeping you as a back-up.
  • The summer shader may become less available, communicate less, and be more vague in communicating with you.
  • Recognize the signs of summer shading as soon as possible so that you don't end up wasting Summer.
Being "Sumemr shaded" can leave you alone and in the dark as to what your significant other is doing.
Source: Connor Scott from Pexels

A rather shady practice may be getting hot around this time of the year. "Summer shading" means the person you are dating deliberately pulls away from you. They reduce communication or contact to enjoy being "single" during the Summer; at the same time, they keep you as an insurance back-up plan. It's a Summer and relationship version of having your cake and eating it too.

Now, assuming that you're not so hot about being someone's backup plan or second, third, or even fourth choice, you probably want to recognize summer-shading as soon as it happens. Otherwise, you may spend the Summer days drifting away with someone who's not so hot about you. Here are the signs that you are being summer-shaded and what to do about it.

The Signs of Summer Shading

The main sign is that there is a significant drop-off in the availability of your partner or whatever romantically he or she is supposed to be for you. Your supposed-to-be partner goes from eager beaver to frequent leaver. Suddenly, fewer plans are made. Many plans may be canceled. Your significant other may become significantly harder to reach.

Naturally, if he or she is hospitalized or trapped in a cave, you don't want to accuse the person of such shading. However, if there is otherwise no clear, justifiable explanation for this change in enthusiasm and behavior, then you've got to wonder what's going on and how interested the other person really is in you.

Vague responses are another clear sign. When people are into you, they will often want to make clear plans with you. Non-committal statements and actions like "we'll see", "maybe", or "I'll get back to you", on the other hand, can strongly suggest that the person is being pretty darn non-committal towards you. That person could be using such vague statements to tie you over and keep you as an option rather than clearly breaking up with you.

A third sign is that the person has clearly stepped up the rest of their schedule—and here's the kicker—without you. Of course, a real kick in the butt would be if the other person were out on dates with other people. But even when there are a lot of parties, concerts, and other events, the big question is: Why aren't you being invited as well?

Ask the Person Directly About Potential Summer Shading

If you notice any of the aforementioned shady signs, it's best to be direct about it. Address your concerns and discuss them with the person directly in a frank and open manner. Don't go in a full force accusation, though, and say something like: "Will the real Summer shady, please stand up." Go in even-keeled and fair with a more information-based approach: "I've noticed that we are spending less time together. Wanted to see if anything has changed." This will give the other person the opportunity to explain and clear up any potential misunderstandings.

Don't Accept Vague Responses

If the other person wants to avoid talking about it, that's a bad sign. My first experience with summer shading was during college when someone hot and heavy during the school year went cold and light on communication during the subsequent Summer. She never offered a straight answer on what had happened. By the Fall, though, it was clear that whatever we had had before the Summer had fallen apart. Maybe she had fallen for someone else. Who knows.

Again, any type of vague response is a bad sign. Perhaps the person says, "Sorry, things have gotten busy." You could respond by asking for specifics in a non-accusatory manner. The more reluctant the person seems to provide direct answers, the shadier it gets. Unless the person is somehow in Fight Club, the person should be able to talk about what's going on with more concrete details.

Establish Your Boundaries and When to Walk Away

Maybe you are fine with being summer-shaded and your Danny Zucco having a Sandy Olsen on the side, or vice-versa, or some other Grease-y situation like that. Perhaps you are engaging in summer shading yourself. Then you could be made for the shade, so to speak.

In all other cases, though, it helps to set your boundaries and be clear to the other person what you expect and are not willing to tolerate. For example, if you want the relationship to be an exclusive one where you regularly see each other, then make that clear. If the other person doesn't want the same, then the two of you are probably not a good fit. It may be best to formally end things. You don't want to have things just fall back in the Fall to how they were before because the other person tried to but couldn't find someone better than you over the Summer.

item.title: Did We Prepare Men for Modern Millennial Marriages?
item.description:
Marriage

Did We Prepare Men for Modern Millennial Marriages?

We told women they could have it all, but did we miss something fundamental?

Posted June 26, 2026

Key points
  • As a society, we changed gender roles faster than we prepared millennial men for what it required of them.
  • Modern marriage demands invisible skills like sharing the mental load and supporting both partners' ambitions.
  • Many millennial men aren't resisting equality—they're navigating roles they were never taught to perform.
  • Recognizing this societal gap is the first step toward closing the millennial marriage gap.

Maybe it’s the social media algorithm pushing content my way, or the fact that what I see in my therapy room as a couples and relationship therapist is a biased sample, since I only work with clients struggling in their relationships. But I have been noticing a theme emerge, both in my clinical work with millennial women and couples, and in what I’m hearing from millennial women online, that is making me wonder if we millennial women can really “have it all” like we were told we could, or did we, as a society, miss a fundamental part of this cultural shift— preparing millennial men for what it would require of them!

Source: Arina Krasnikova / Pexels

Millennials Are Doing Marriages Differently

Research clearly shows that millennials are marrying differently from the generations before. Millennials are marrying later, are more selective about marriage, and are contributing to a decline in overall divorce rates in the U.S. (Parker & Stepler, 2020; Cohen, 2019). They also ask more of marriage than any other generation before them. They expect emotional intimacy, friendship, equality, shared parenting, and mutual support for both partners’ ambitions. In many ways, the bar for what constitutes a successful marriage has never been higher.

However, as millennial couples enter midlife, become parents, and take on bigger roles in their careers, I am seeing increasing tension around gender roles in their marriages. Many millennial women are sharing that they increasingly feel a sense of hopelessness about their husbands meeting their needs, and some are coming to the realization that their husbands simply do not have the skills they need from their partners.

So why are millennial couples experiencing tension around gender roles in midlife, when both partners were previously fundamentally on the same page in their beliefs around gender equality?

Equality in Theory Is Different From Equality in Practice

Research actually shows that among millennials, 72 percent believe the most satisfying marriage is one in which both partners work and both share household and childcare responsibilities (Parker & Wang, 2011). As a therapist having an intimate inside view of what’s happening in millennial marriages, I don’t think millennial marriages are struggling because men don’t believe in equality. I think many are struggling because society changed women’s opportunities through the tireless work of the feminist movement, but we didn’t prepare men for what gender equality would practically require of them.

The Marriage Gap No One Prepared Millennials For

The reality is that many millennial couples are navigating a mismatch: the millennial marriage gap. They aspire to be in an egalitarian partnership, but many men were not raised with models of what practical and emotional equality looks like in a marriage.

While the second-wave feminist movement did a great job at teaching millennial boys that women could do everything they could, we missed out on the very important part of this puzzle—that to create a society where women will take on big careers and ambitions, men will also need to be taught to do everything women traditionally did!

Millennial boys, who are now husbands, needed to be taught the practical skills that are required to support a partner and a family as an equal partner, such nurturing children through babysitting, playing house, learning to bake, cook, clean, and organize their spaces or at least be exposed to all this as being relevant to them, not just a “moms and girls thing.”

But I also don’t want to oversimplify what preparing boys for these family roles would have looked like. It’s not simply knowing how to cook or clean. It’s learning to anticipate that daycare paperwork needs to be completed before the deadline. It’s noticing when the refrigerator is empty, or the diaper bag needs restocking. It’s about rearranging your work schedule because your partner has an important meeting, rather than assuming your wife will figure it out. It’s carrying some of the invisible emotional labor of running a family—remembering birthdays, scheduling doctor’s appointments, planning holidays. Growing up, most millennial men saw their mothers take on the role of manager and anchor of the household, despite their having careers and increased opportunities for women in the workplace.

Research suggests that children learn more about gender roles from parents’ everyday behaviors—such as how childcare, household labor, and paid work are divided—than from what parents say they believe about gender equality (Halpern & Perry-Jenkins, 2016). In many families, girls absorbed this role over years of watching mothers and grandmothers anticipate needs, manage households, shoulder the emotional labor, and often place the needs of others before their own. Millennial girls growing up were still also more likely to be expected to help—to babysit younger siblings, assist with cooking, tidy shared spaces, and notice what needed to be done. Many boys, by contrast, were growing up with far fewer opportunities to observe or practice these same responsibilities.

Where Do We Go From Here?

There is an age-old saying that behind every successful man is a strong woman. However, as a society, we conveniently forgot that behind every successful woman, there also needs to be an emotionally and practically supportive man. As a couple, if we can recognize this societal lapse, instead of pointing fingers at each other or playing the blame game, it can help women be more compassionate in asking for more of their partners, and it can help men feel more motivated to make the effort of learning what they should have been taught to begin with.

Many men already had a role model for proactive household management and emotional caregiving; however, in most families, it was just their mothers, not their dads. Most millennial men saw their mothers take on this role. Instead of feeling lost in what is expected of them, they can now ask themselves, “What would my mother have already noticed or done by now in this situation? How did she carry the household?” and maybe try to do that!

Hopefully, we will also do better at raising the next generation of boys: raising them with the skills to be the partners our daughters will need in their marriages, and more importantly, modeling the modern gender roles that will set them up for success in their marriages as men.

item.title: Overthinking's 3 Darkest Disguises
item.description:
Self-Help

Overthinking's 3 Darkest Disguises

You've been fighting the symptoms, here's the source.

Posted June 26, 2026

Key points
  • Overthinking is a shape-shifter because it can appear as anxiety, depression, or as being stuck.
  • Overthinking starts out feeling like a solution but it becomes a trap that sucks you in deeper and deeper.
  • The fix is the same for all three. Change your relationship with your thoughts not the thoughts themselves.

One psychological process is running the show in people's lives more than most therapists realize. After decades of working with children, teens, and adults, I have come to believe that overthinking is one of the most underestimated forces of human suffering. Not because it is common, but because it is transdiagnostic. That is psychologist-speak for a mental habit that cuts across several psychological disorders rather than belonging to just one.

If you have ever wondered why therapy often helps with one issue only to have another one surface, this may be why. What I am saying is that overthinking is a shape-shifter. It doesn't always look like overthinking—it looks like your problem.

Let's now take a look at the three darkest disguises of overthinking.

1. Anxiety

Anxiety says things like, "What if something bad happens?" or "What if I am making a mistake?" That can feel like caution or even preparation, but underneath it is your mind running (looping, actually) through worst-case scenarios. This process is really about searching for the certainty that never arrives. Said another way, the more you try to think of yourself to safety, the less safe you feel. Instead of protecting anxious people, it feeds their fear. A client I'll call Sara, a 34-year-old information technology team lead, spent hours each night rehearsing what could go wrong the next day. She erroneously believed this would make her more prepared. In reality, it left her feeling drained and impatient, and convinced her workplace was more dysfunctional than it actually was.

2. Depression

Depression says, "Why did this happen to me?" It feels like a reflection, as if "processing the past" can lead to deeper understanding for the future. But incessant rumination is a form of overthinking that is particularly emotionally disruptive. The depressed mind rehashes and replays past hurts and disappointments without any constructive problem-solving to release oneself from the past. In this case, more thinking does not create valuable insight; rather, it deepens the rut and creates a dark hole that takes a huge emotional toll.

This was exemplified by a client I will refer to as Scott. He came to see me months after his divorce and was stuck replaying painful past conversations, arguments, and disappointments. Scott's mantra is, "I just need to understand what went wrong." But in his case, he became so mired in overthinking that he could not truly understand what led to the demise of his marriage. He was stuck in overthinking.

3. Failure To Launch

It really bothers me how often failure to launch is misread as "laziness" or "lack of motivation". I have worked with many adult children with "failure to launch," and the common denominator I have seen is overthinking. In fact, when I was reflecting on my experience of writing Freeing Your Child From Overthinking, I saw with striking clarity that the adult children who can't move forward are often consumed by questions such as: "What if I can't make it in the real world?" or "What if I choose the wrong path?"

In this case, overthinking wears the mask of deliberation, but in reality, it steals months or even years of the lives of struggling adult children. A client I will refer to as Mike had a college degree and a supportive family. He also had 23 browser tabs open on his laptop, filled with companies and jobs he had been "researching" for the past two years. He was emotionally paralyzed by the quest for certainty that overthinking will not deliver.

The Cruel Irony—and the Way Out

Overthinking starts as a solution by driving us to more analysis, more replying, and more rehearsing. Yet it delivers the opposite of what it promises. The real problem is not your thoughts but rather the relationship you have with them. When you stop treating every thought as a crisis to fear, you feel liberated. That's because you begin to tolerate uncertainty and move forward even though whatever you're striving for may not feel perfect. Anxiety, depression, and emotional paralysis don't need separate fixes because they have one transdiagnostic engine. And, you can cut off the fuel source.
